questions.title: How does the Eighth Circuit distinguish 'intrinsic' firearm-possession evidence from Rule 404(b) propensity evidence?
questions.question_body: The panel allowed D.F. and C.F. to testify that they had seen the same sawed-off Marlin .22 rifle in Cutbank’s possession on earlier occasions, treating that as intrinsic evidence of the charged § 922(g) possession and citing United States v. Battle. What makes prior sightings of the same gun 'intrinsic' rather than 404(b) propensity evidence? Do courts require some threshold showing that it is in fact the same specific firearm (e.g., serial number, unique features), or will a witness’s identification based on appearance suffice? How does the 'continuous possession' concept work in this context, and does Rule 403 balancing still apply even if the evidence is labeled intrinsic?

questions.title: Was a contemporaneous limiting instruction required when officers relayed D.F.’s out-of-court statements before she testified?
questions.question_body: Before trial, the defense asked the court to instruct the jury not to consider D.F.’s statements to police as substantive evidence until D.F. testified, to avoid hearsay/Confrontation issues. The court declined, and the panel later said no hearsay was admitted and the Confrontation Clause was satisfied because D.F. ultimately testified. Are officers’ references to a victim’s statements admissible to show context/why police acted, and if so is a limiting instruction typically required at that time? If the statements were 'testimonial' under Crawford, does the declarant’s later in-court testimony cure any Confrontation problem stemming from earlier admission? What standard of review applies to the refusal to give a contemporaneous limiting instruction, and how much preservation was needed here?

questions.title: Did the court properly deny the motion to strike D.F.’s remark that her sister was killed by a gun under Rule 403?
questions.question_body: On cross about inconsistencies, D.F. volunteered that she dislikes guns because her sister was killed by one. The court denied the motion to strike, and the panel found no unfair prejudice. How do courts assess the risk of unfair prejudice from emotionally charged background facts like a family member’s death, especially when they could bolster the witness’s credibility or evoke sympathy? Does it matter that the defense elicited the context on cross? Is a sua sponte curative instruction expected in this situation, and under what circumstances would admitting such a remark be reversible error under Rule 403?

questions.title: Can defense impeach with a police report the witness didn’t author? What foundation is required under Rules 613 and 901?
questions.question_body: The judge allowed questions about C.F.’s prior inconsistent statements to an investigator but barred defense counsel from reading from the police report because C.F. didn’t write it, citing authentication concerns. Under Rule 613(b), can counsel confront the witness by quoting the report’s language if the witness acknowledges speaking to the officer? Must the officer (or report author) testify to authenticate the report under Rule 901, or can the defense use it as impeachment-only without offering it for the truth? Could the report come in as a recorded recollection (803(5)) or public/business record (803(6)/(8)) for impeachment purposes, and how is hearsay within hearsay handled when the goal is only to impeach?

questions.title: What qualifies as 'another felony offense' for § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) on these facts, and what evidentiary showing is needed?
questions.question_body: The court adopted PSR facts and concluded the gun was used 'in connection with another felony,' but the opinion doesn’t identify which felony (e.g., domestic assault, kidnapping/false imprisonment, burglary/trespass at the garage, assault on an officer). In the Eighth Circuit, does 'in connection with' require that the firearm facilitate the other felony (nexus/facilitation), or is contemporaneous possession during the felony enough? What is the standard of proof at sentencing, and can uncharged conduct described in a PSR—supported by hearsay—alone establish the enhancement if the defendant lodges no factual objection? Would a legal objection (but no factual objection) preserve a challenge to applying the enhancement?

questions.title: Is there impermissible double counting when both ACCA status and § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) drive the offense level, with § 4B1.4 picking the higher?
questions.question_body: Here, ACCA would set the offense level at 34 under § 4B1.4, but enhancements under § 2K2.1 (including (b)(6)(B)) yielded 35, so the court applied § 4B1.4(b)’s 'greater offense level applies' rule. Does the Guidelines framework expressly authorize using § 2K2.1 enhancements to displace the ACCA-specific guideline, or is there a double-counting concern when prior violent felonies both trigger ACCA and provide predicates for higher base levels/enhancements under § 2K2.1? Is there controlling Eighth Circuit precedent on whether it is proper to apply § 2K2.1 enhancements in ACCA cases when § 4B1.4 also applies?

questions.title: What are the preservation and standard-of-review consequences when the defendant adopts the PSR and cites little authority on appeal?
questions.question_body: The panel notes that Cutbank 'provid[ed] no cases and almost no analysis' and that he adopted the PSR’s factual statements without objection. Should unpreserved evidentiary objections or sentencing fact disputes be reviewed only for plain error? Can the appellate court affirm for lack of prejudice without first expressly applying plain-error review? By adopting the PSR facts, did Cutbank waive only factual disputes or also his ability to raise purely legal challenges to the § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) enhancement based on those facts?

questions.title: How does harmless-error and cumulative-error analysis interact with potential Confrontation Clause violations?
questions.question_body: The court concludes there was no hearsay admitted and D.F. testified, then says any evidentiary errors were harmless in light of strong evidence and rejects cumulative-error claims. If there had been a Confrontation Clause error, would the Eighth Circuit apply the Chapman 'harmless beyond a reasonable doubt' standard rather than the usual evidentiary harmlessness test? When multiple alleged errors include both constitutional and non-constitutional claims, how does the cumulative-error doctrine assess prejudice—does it aggregate under a single constitutional harmlessness standard, or treat each type of error under its respective standard?
